caption.text: A slot in the pig’s back once admitted coins; a modeled chain and padlock announce its purpose. In Majapahit Java, an animal’s body became a personal treasury. Its survival is unusual because retrieving coins often meant breaking the vessel.

proposals.reason: A documented animal form serves as a coin container; the modeled bank symbols and unusual unbroken survival make the exhibition connection specific.

caption.text: This dragon’s body is molded from green ink. Ink cakes were normally ground with water for painting and calligraphy; this ornamental example belongs to an unused set. Its sculptural detail preserves a material usually made to dissolve.

proposals.reason: The art is molded ink rather than jade or carved stone; the material and unused condition make surface and function unusually revealing.

caption.text: Thorvaldsen modeled Byron in 1835. This unglazed porcelain version, possibly by David Ivanovitch Jensen, shows the poet seated with Childe Harold and a broken column. Such copies carried the sculptural image into collections far from the marble at Trinity College, Cambridge.

proposals.reason: An explicitly identified porcelain copy offers a strong example of how a sculpture survives and circulates through material translation; uncertain copy authorship is retained.
